app.title: ATP Fatigue Forecaster
app.summary: A person picks two competitors from a looked-up roster, or types in their rank, recent workload, rest, form and head-to-head values by hand, chooses the playing surface, and runs the inference. They get a split win-probability bar, the predicted winner with a confidence level, and generated commentary that ties the load, rest and form differences to a fatigue framework. Two what-if sweeps then show how the probability would move with more rest for one side or a different 28-day load for the other. Further tabs check that the model is worth trusting: its scores against simple rank baselines, ROC and calibration curves, feature importance, and an ablation that adds feature groups one at a time. A separate tab estimates the win probability from a live score state alone.

task.text: Predict which of two competitors wins from pre-match workload, rest and form features, and test whether those features add predictive signal beyond ranking alone.

data.text: Historical match records with dates, ranks, surface, round and duration, turned into rolling pre-match workload, rest, form and head-to-head features for each side; plus point-by-point score logs for a second, score-state model.
data.item: one match between two competitors, described by each side's features from before the match

stage.text: analysing match records with a trained forecasting model and checking that the load features hold up against baselines

mechanism.text: A sidebar form fills in each side's features, either from a roster lookup or from manual sliders, and the inference tab turns them into a probability bar, a radar comparison, commentary and counterfactual sweep curves. Separate validation tabs show the same trained model against baselines and as a staged feature ablation, and an in-match tab recomputes the probability live as the score-state inputs change.

field.text: match-outcome forecasting from training-load features with ablation testing, in sports science

workflow.name: predict a two-sided outcome with a trained model and test which feature groups add signal

steps.here: Match seasons are fetched from a pinned source and turned into rolling pre-match features, built in date and match order so no window includes the match being predicted; a freshness badge shows how recent the data is

steps.step: set up the two items to compare
steps.here: The sidebar switches between Player Lookup, which fills both sides' stats and head-to-head from history, and Manual Entry, with sliders for rank, 7/14/28-day minutes, rest days, form and head-to-head; a surface picker applies to both

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: Run Inference sends the features to a calibrated gradient-boosting model, which gives a split probability bar, predicted winner, a HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW confidence label, surface, and commentary on the load, rest, head-to-head and surface differences

steps.step: vary one input and watch the prediction respond
steps.here: What-if curves sweep 0–14 extra rest days for one side and 0–1200 minutes of 28-day load for the other, holding everything else fixed, and report the largest change

steps.step: compare the model against simpler baselines
steps.here: Accuracy, ROC-AUC, CV AUC, Brier and log loss on a chronological hold-out, a table and ROC curves against higher-rank, rank-logistic and Elo-style baselines, a reliability diagram, and the top-10 feature importances

steps.step: add feature groups one at a time and measure the lift
steps.here: Bars of test AUC for ranking only, then adding load, form, head-to-head and opponent quality, and finally the full set, with the change from each step and a hypothesis-result verdict

steps.step: estimate the outcome from the current state
steps.here: Format, server, sets, games and point number go into a score-state model trained on point-by-point data; it returns a live probability bar and a curve across 0–6 games in the current set

distinctive: Workload is cumulative minutes in 7, 14 and 28-day windows, weighted by surface and round multipliers

Leakage guards: features are computed before each match enters a player's history, the sort is stable within a tournament, labels for the two sides are randomised, and the in-match model is split by match rather than by point
A staged ablation tests a stated research hypothesis: does load add signal beyond rank?
The pre-match model is isotonic-calibrated and checked with a reliability diagram, while the in-match model is deliberately left uncalibrated
Commentary maps each feature difference onto the stages of a fatigue cascade taken from a systematic review
